Two things: the VM is faster, and a compiled file can be made hard to read.

### Comparisons are instructions now

A call to `<` costs a type assertion on the operator, an arity check and an
indirect call through the primitive's function pointer — once per comparison,
which in a loop is once per iteration.  The compiler emits an instruction
instead wherever it can see that the operator is still the interpreter's own
binding; a program that rebinds `<` gets the call it asked for, and one that
compares a flonum or a bignum falls back to the primitive, so the numeric tower
is never reimplemented and nothing behaves differently.

Measured on the twelve benchmarks, pinned to one core, best of nine:

| | before | after | |
|---|---|---|---|
| `locals` | 69.62 ms | 62.36 ms | −10.4% |
| `vectors` | 36.04 ms | 32.12 ms | −10.9% |
| `globals` | 71.56 ms | 64.34 ms | −10.1% |
| `tail-loop` | 62.73 ms | 56.60 ms | −9.8% |
| `sort` | 12.17 ms | 11.28 ms | −7.3% |
| `fib` | 9.59 ms | 8.96 ms | −6.6% |

**Geometric mean 5.8% faster**, eleven of twelve workloads improved or level.
(A second run of the same binaries measured 8.1%; the machine is shared, and the
two runs bracket the answer.)

`+`, `-` and `*` were made instructions too, in the same way, and **measured 22%
slower** — they are variadic primitives whose body is already a tight loop, so
an instruction that tests its operands and then falls back to the same primitive
costs more than the call it saves.  They were removed rather than kept behind a
flag, and the measurement is in [docs/bytecode-internals.md](docs/bytecode-internals.md)
so that nobody re-adds them.

The bytecode format is **version 4** because of the new opcodes.  Files written
by earlier versions are still read; the disassembler has their names.

### `goscheme compile -obfuscate`

A compiled file carries more than its instructions: every body has a name, every
slot has the name of the variable in it, and every global reference is a symbol.
None of that is needed to run the program, and all of it says what the program
is — a slot called `password` next to a call to `string=?` is a sentence.

```sh
goscheme compile prog.scm -o prog.scmc -obfuscate
```

* compiled bodies are renamed `b0`, `b1`, …;
* slot names become `v0`, `v1`, … — they stay, one per slot, because
  `opLocalCheck` uses them to say which variable was used before it was
  initialized: the message survives and the name in it does not;
* each constant pool is shuffled and the instructions that index it are
  rewritten, so compiling twice gives different bytes and the position of a
  constant says nothing;
* the globals the program defines are renamed, where it can be shown that
  nothing else refers to them by name — a name mentioned in a source chunk keeps
  its name, because that chunk is evaluated by the interpreter as written.

### The usage now lists it

`goscheme -h` said only `goscheme compile <script> [-o <output.scmc>]`, so the
one place a user looks for the new flag did not have it.  The options are
grouped by subcommand now, which also settles a collision a single list could
not: `-i` means "enter the REPL" to `goscheme` and "the interpreter to copy" to
`goscheme build`.  A test reads the usage lines back and asserts that each
option is on the line it belongs to.

It is not encryption and does not pretend to be: the strings and numbers the
program works with are still in the file, because it needs them, and a reader
can still follow the instructions.  What goes is the vocabulary.  Obfuscation
costs nothing at run time (10.32 ms against 10.58 ms for `sort`), and the file
is a `.scmc` file like any other — the interpreter reads it without knowing.
